name: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)
tagline: Isolating core domain logic inside an explicit boundary where HTTP, SQL, queues, and external APIs plug in through domain-owned interfaces.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of Hexagonal Architecture—from driving vs. driven ports and the inward Dependency Rule to ArchUnit enforcement and contract testing.

spark.summary: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters) isolates core domain logic inside an explicit boundary where all external I/O—HTTP, SQL, queues, third-party APIs—plugs in through interfaces owned by the domain.
spark.keyTakeaway: By inverting dependencies so adapters depend on domain ports (never the reverse), you can swap databases, frameworks, or message brokers and run full business-logic tests in milliseconds with zero infrastructure.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** In traditional layered architectures (`Controller -> Service -> Repository -> DB`), business rules inevitably leak ORM annotations (`@Entity`, `@Transactional`) and HTTP status codes.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Driving Adapters -> Domain Core (Ports) <- Driven Adapters (REST / Kafka / CLI -> Domain Core & Ports -> Postgres / Stripe -> Anti-Corruption Layer); In-Memory Fast Suite + Postgres Contract Suite + Import Linter (PR / CI -> ArchUnit / Linter -> Domain + Fakes -> Postgres Container).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Compare architectural styles by coupling, test speed, and ceremony. Without automated enforcement, developers inevitably import `sqlalchemy` or `spring-web` inside `domain/`.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Apply clean boundaries and state machines in concrete LLD and microservice architecture problems.

learningJourney.title: What is Hexagonal Architecture
learningJourney.explanation:
In traditional layered architectures (`Controller -> Service -> Repository -> DB`), business rules inevitably leak ORM annotations (`@Entity`, `@Transactional`) and HTTP status codes. **Hexagonal Architecture** (Alistair Cockburn) draws a strict boundary around the application core:

- **Driving (Primary) Ports**: Interfaces exposed *by* the core (`PlaceOrderUseCase`), called by **Driving Adapters** (REST controller, gRPC handler, Kafka listener).
- **Driven (Secondary) Ports**: Interfaces defined *by* the core for what it needs (`OrderRepository`, `PaymentGateway`), implemented by **Driven Adapters** (Postgres, Stripe, in-memory fakes).
- **The Dependency Rule**: Source-code imports point strictly **inward** (`adapters -> application -> domain`).

learningJourney.title: Why Decoupling Domain Invariants from Frameworks Pays Off
learningJourney.explanation: Web frameworks and ORMs churn every few years, while core billing, ledger, and risk-scoring invariants endure for decades. Hexagonal Architecture lets you swap Stripe for Adyen, or wrap a messy legacy ERP behind an **Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)** without polluting domain models.

ideas.description: Run a shared **contract test suite** against both the in-memory fake (on every save) and the real Postgres adapter (in CI) so fakes never diverge from real SQL behavior.

Use full Hexagonal ports for commands/writes with invariants, while letting read queries hit optimized SQL views directly.
costs: Read models bypass domain entities, requiring discipline not to sneak mutations into read paths.

benefits: Direct SQL/dbt or simple layered handlers avoid pointless pass-through interfaces.
costs: Wrapping 1-to-1 table CRUD in 4 layers of ports and DTOs creates pure boilerplate.

learningJourney.title: Domain Ports, Pure Domain Models & Unit-of-Work Boundaries
learningJourney.explanation: Keep domain entities as plain dataclasses/POJOs/structs, and keep transaction boundaries explicit via a `UnitOfWork` port so hiding persistence behind a `Repository` never accidentally splits an atomic write across two transactions.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```python
from typing import Protocol
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Order:
    order_id: str
    total_cents: int

class OrderRepositoryPort(Protocol):  # Driven Port owned by domain
    def save(self, order: Order) -> None: ...

class PaymentGatewayPort(Protocol):   # Driven Port owned by domain
    def charge(self, order_id: str, cents: int) -> str: ...

class PlaceOrderUseCase:              # Pure domain service (zero framework imports)
    def __init__(self, repo: OrderRepositoryPort, payments: PaymentGatewayPort):
        self._repo = repo
        self._payments = payments

    def execute(self, order_id: str, cents: int) -> str:
        if cents <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Order total must be positive")
        tx_id = self._payments.charge(order_id, cents)
        self._repo.save(Order(order_id=order_id, total_cents=cents))
        return tx_id
```

options.text: The domain core owns `OrderRepository`; the risk is that the in-memory fake can drift from real PostgreSQL constraint/transaction behavior unless verified by a shared contract test suite
options.feedback: Correct: domain ownership inverts the dependency, and contract tests keep fakes faithful to real SQL adapters.

options.text: The PostgreSQL adapter owns `OrderRepository`; the risk is slow unit tests
options.feedback: Driven ports are always owned by the domain core, not the adapter.

options.text: The REST controller owns `OrderRepository`; the risk is HTTP 502 errors
options.feedback: Controllers are driving adapters and do not own persistence ports.
